title: When Retrieval Practice Goes Wrong
author: David Didau
summary: Retrieval practice has become a mandated best practice, yet often mutates into time-wasting rituals. The 'five disconnected questions at the start of lesson' orthodoxy misses the point: retrieval is not generically good. It works because it increases accessibility of knowledge at the point it is needed. When retrieved knowledge is immediately applied, both performance in the moment and memory over time strengthen. When disconnected from the lesson to follow, retrieval becomes empty ceremony. The article explains Bjork's New Theory of Disuse and the concept of desirable difficulty—tasks that require effort without tipping into failure—and argues that recall starters should aim for near-universal success, not failure that compounds low student self-esteem.
points: Retrieval practice works because it increases accessibility of knowledge when needed; disconnected retrieval is wasted effort.
Desirable difficulty is not struggle for its own sake—it's effortful success that strengthens memory.
Failure at the start of a lesson is corrosive and compounds; recall starters should aim for near-universal success with prompts until retrieval succeeds.
Effective recall starters follow three rules: 100% student success, questions immediately useful in the lesson, and regular repetition to build fluency.
quotes: Whatever the benefits of interleaving might be, the Do Now is possibly not the best place to try to harness them.
A desirable difficulty is a task that requires effort without tipping into failure. It slows performance in the short term, but strengthens retention and transfer over time.
What strengthens memory is not struggle for its own sake, but effortful success.” Archived from David Didau on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
